t.1.221.1: Then, as the fire blazed up, those Śārṅgakas, deeply distressed, tormented and utterly terrified, found no refuge.
t.1.221.2: Seeing her little sons, mere children, their wretched mother Jaritā, scorched by grief, lamented, O lord of men.
t.1.221.3: This terrifying fire, burning the brushwood, has set out and is coming upon us; dreadful, setting the whole world ablaze, it deepens my sorrow.
t.1.221.6: I am not able to abandon them, and my heart seems to burn within me. Which son should I forsake, and which son should I take with me as I go?
t.1.221.5: Because they are without strength, my sons are not able to go when I go; and I am not able to take my sons and move elsewhere.
t.1.221.4: These dull-witted children torment me, featherless and without feet, yet they are the sole refuge of our forefathers. And here this fire comes, spreading terror and licking at the trees.
t.1.221.7: What should I do, and what would it accomplish? Think, my little sons, how it might be done. Though I ponder it, I find no means of release for you at all, so I shall cover you with my limbs and meet death together with you.
t.1.221.8: For this lineage rests upon Jaritāri by virtue of his being the eldest, and Sārisṛkka may beget offspring as the one who increases the family of the forefathers.
t.1.221.9: "Stambamitra shall practise austerities, and Droṇa shall be the foremost knower of brahman." Having spoken thus, your pitiless father went away long ago.
t.1.221.11: By her own wisdom she then saw no means of escape from the fire for her sons. Then those Śārṅgas replied to their mother as she spoke thus.
t.1.221.12: Casting off your affection, mother, fly to where the fire does not reach; for if we perish, you will have other sons, but if you perish, mother, there would be no continuation of our family.
t.1.221.10: "Taking up which one could I manage to get away? Whose is this supreme calamity? What could I do so that the needful thing would be done?" Thus she was distraught.
t.1.221.13: Having considered both of these, whatever would be fitting for our family, that, mother, you should do, for this would be the highest time for you to do it.
t.1.221.15: Here in the ground, near this tree, is the hole of a rat; enter it quickly, for there you will have no fear of the fire.
t.1.221.14: Do not let your affection for us, your sons, bring about the destruction of the family, for this deed of our father, who longed for the higher worlds, must not be in vain.
t.1.221.16: Then I shall cover the hole with dust, my little sons; this, I think, is the remedy against the blazing fire whose path is black.
t.1.221.17: Then, when the fire has passed, I will come to clear away the heap of dust. Let this plan please you as a means of escape from the fire.
t.1.221.18: A flesh-eating rat would destroy us, featherless as we are and no more than lumps of flesh. Seeing this danger, we shall not be able to take refuge there.
t.1.221.19: How might the fire not burn us, and how might the rat not devour us? How might our father not be left without issue, and how might our mother be kept alive?
t.1.221.20: In the hole there would be destruction from the rat, and for those who range through the sky, destruction from the fire. Having weighed both of these, burning is better, not being eaten.
t.1.221.21: Death would be shameful for us if a rat were to devour us in the hole; giving up the body through the fire, sanctioned by the virtuous, is what we desire.
